outcome: No source found since 26 January 2024 classifies pairs of n×n matrices under simultaneous conjugation in the sense the bullet asks; the window holds a finite-field polynomial-time canonical-form algorithm (Qiao and Sun, FOCS 2024), a non-existence result for one type of normal form for pairs (Bongartz, Feb 2025), a centralizer result claimed to solve a 'weaker version of the Wild Problem' (Bouarga and Charkani, Feb 2025), and a January 2026 preprint by Bongartz and Friedland claiming complete invariants for all p-tuples over any field, which its own authors say is not an explicit solution and which has had no human review.
problem_asks: (a) Classify PAIRS (A,B) of square matrices (two matrices, not tuples). (b) Of size n×n, for all n (the statement gives no bound on n). (c) Up to simultaneous conjugation (A,B) ↦ (S⁻¹AS, S⁻¹BS), S invertible of the same size. (d) 'Classification' means a complete description of the set of orbits (for example a list of canonical forms, or a parametrised normal form). The statement does not name a field; the wild framing used for the problem (and linked from Wikipedia) is over an arbitrary field, so the field is left open here. Not asked by the statement: counting orbits, commuting or nilpotent pairs, tuples of three or more matrices, other equivalence relations (congruence, unitary, polynomial, left-right), or tame/wild status as such. Wikipedia's list places the bullet under Algebra with a link to the 'Wild problem' article, which defines wildness by containment of this pair problem.

events.what_happened: I. M. Gel'fand and V. A. Ponomarev, 'Remarks on the classification of a pair of commuting linear transformations in a finite-dimensional space', Funct. Anal. Appl. 3:4 (1969), pp. 81-82. Later papers read the note as showing that classifying commuting nilpotent pairs under similarity contains classifying arbitrary t-tuples of operators; this containment is the origin of the 'wild' label for that subclass and is cited as the foundation of the wildness benchmark. Only the mathnet record was opened (title, pages, DOI, received 23.06.1969, no abstract); the note's own statement was not read, so its content here is as described by Bondarenko-Futorny-Petravchuk-Sergeichuk (arXiv 2012.04038) and Hua (arXiv 2303.15862).
events.delivers: Containment only: classifying commuting nilpotent pairs under similarity is at least as hard as classifying t-tuples of operators, so the commuting-nilpotent pair problem is wild. Classifies no pairs.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The note concerns commuting nilpotent pairs, a subclass of the bullet's pairs, and gives no classification of any class.

checked_by.who: V. M. Bondarenko, V. Futorny, A. P. Petravchuk, V. V. Sergeichuk
checked_by.qualification: Specialists in matrix problems and representation theory publishing in Linear Algebra and its Applications
checked_by.what_they_did: Restate the Gelfand-Ponomarev containment (for commuting nilpotent pairs, and for the case where the common kernel is one-dimensional, classify a subclass with a normal form); the abstract says the problem 'is considered as hopeless'. They do not re-verify the 1969 argument in the abstract

events.direction: Toward hopelessness: establishes wildness (containment) for commuting nilpotent pairs. It does not settle the problem either way.

events.what_happened: S. Friedland, 'Simultaneous similarity of matrices', Adv. Math. 50 (1983), 189-265. NOT OPENED: the Adv. Math. article was not reachable and the DTIC copy of the associated Mathematics Research Center report (ADA114536) returned HTTP 403. Secondary descriptions conflict. A search summary of Belitskii-Sergeichuk (arXiv 0709.2488) says Friedland gave a complete set of invariants for pairs under simultaneous similarity. Other secondary descriptions (search summaries, a 2009 tribute preface, the 2026 Bongartz-Friedland preprint's background) say Friedland gave a finite collection of invariants that determine an orbit only up to finite ambiguity. Bongartz (arXiv 2502.10926) cites Friedland 1983 as the work his pair-of-2x2 analysis is 'more precise than'. An earlier MRC technical summary report with the same title (1982) is reported in secondary sources and was not checked.
events.revisions: An MRC technical summary report of the same title is reported with a 1982 date in a search summary; not verified.
events.delivers: Unknown from the material opened. Per the more common secondary description: invariants that characterise a pair's similarity orbit only up to a finite ambiguity, i.e. a partial classification. Per one secondary description: a complete set of invariants. These two readings are not reconciled.
events.remains: If the finite-ambiguity reading holds: classification of pairs up to that ambiguity, not classification of the orbits themselves. If the complete reading holds: whether the invariants are explicit enough to count as a classification. Either way the statement's classification is not delivered as a list or parametrisation of orbits according to the secondary sources.

events.what_happened: G. R. Belitskii and V. V. Sergeichuk, 'Complexity of matrix problems', Linear Algebra Appl. 361 (2003), 203-222 (arXiv 0709.2488, posted 16 Sep 2007 as a re-posting). The paper uses the pair problem as the benchmark for wildness: it shows the pair problem contains every classification problem given by quivers or posets, so all wild quiver or poset problems have the same complexity and a solution of one solves all. It also shows the pair problem is contained in, but does not contain, classification of three-valent tensors. Abstract opened; full text not read.
events.revisions: arXiv 0709.2488 v1 16 Sep 2007 is a re-posting; the journal version (2003) carries the first public written argument.
events.delivers: Establishes the pair problem as the complexity benchmark for wildness and shows its equivalence with the quiver and poset wild problems. It does not classify pairs.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.

The pair problem is used as the benchmark throughout. Abstract opened.

A search summary claimed it relaxes PAP⁻¹ = A' to PA = A'P, dropping invertibility of P; that claim was not verified in the opened abstract. No journal reference listed.

events.what_happened: S. Kouchekian and B. Shektman, 'On simultaneous similarity of families of commuting operators', arXiv 2305.01196 (v1 2 May 2023), math.FA. Gives a criterion for simultaneous similarity of m-tuples of k-cyclic commuting operators on an arbitrary Banach space, with an equivalence condition for finite-dimensional spaces and applications to commuting square matrices. The abstract calls the general commuting-family problem open even in finite dimensions, 'a wild problem in linear algebra'.
events.delivers: A criterion for simultaneous similarity of commuting k-cyclic families, in finite and infinite dimension. It does not treat arbitrary pairs.
events.remains: Non-commuting pairs and commuting pairs that are not k-cyclic.

events.what_happened: U. B. Sharma, 'Simultaneous Similarity Classes of Commuting matrices over a finite field', arXiv 1409.2698 (v1 7 Sep 2014; latest v7 5 Apr 2016), math.AC. Counts similarity classes of commuting k-tuples of n×n matrices over F_q, equivalently isomorphism classes of n-dimensional modules over F_q[x_1,...,x_k]. The generating function in k is shown rational, and computed for n ≤ 4, with coefficients polynomial in q with non-negative integer coefficients. Abstract opened.

events.what_happened: T. G. Gerasimova, R. A. Horn, V. V. Sergeichuk, 'Simultaneous unitary equivalences', arXiv 1112.4446 (19 Dec 2011), Linear Algebra Appl. 438 (2013), 3829-3835. Gives an algorithm with finitely many computations to decide whether one unitary matrix U simultaneously carries finite sets of pairs of n×n complex matrices into unitary similarity or unitary congruence (via U or its conjugate). The equivalence is unitary, not general simultaneous similarity.
events.delivers: A decision algorithm for a unitary variant of simultaneous equivalence of pairs of complex matrices. It is an analogue with a different equivalence, not simultaneous similarity by arbitrary invertibles.
events.remains: The problem as stated (general invertible simultaneous conjugation).

events.what_happened: H. Derksen, I. Klep, V. Makam, J. Volčič, 'Ranks of linear matrix pencils separate simultaneous similarity orbits', arXiv 2109.09418 (v1 20 Sep 2021); Adv. Math. 415 (2023), 108888. Evaluates linear matrix pencils on tuples and shows that the ranks of these pencils separate simultaneous similarity orbits: two n×n tuples are simultaneously similar exactly when all such ranks agree. The paper's default (Section 2) imposes no extra field hypothesis, and Theorem 1.1 is stated without one; Section 4 assumes algebraically closed characteristic 0 or real closed fields for other results. Corollary 3.5 bounds the size of the pencils by n^3+n, independent of the number of matrices, so the family of rank invariants is finite but very large. The paper calls the result 'separating invariants', not classification, and says the classification of matrix tuples up to similarity has been deemed hopeless (citing Le Bruyn). Full text read through the HTML fetch.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 20 Sep 2021; published Adv. Math. 415 (2023) 108888 (version differences not compared).
events.delivers: Complete separating invariants for simultaneous similarity of p-tuples of n×n matrices (pairs included as p = 2): the ranks of a finite (size-bounded) family of linear matrix pencils built from the tuple. Per Theorem 1.1, with no field restriction stated. Not a normal form, parametrisation or explicit orbit list. The paper calls it separation, not classification.
events.remains: An explicit classification in the normal-form or parametrisation sense of the bullet: no list of orbits or canonical forms is given. The pencil-rank invariants are not reduced to a set of normal forms.
events.doubts: The invariant family is indexed by all pencils up to size n^3+n: complete but not explicit. Whether a separating invariant family counts as classifying orbits is a question about the bullet's meaning, not a defect of the proof. Pith lists no review of this paper.
events.direction: Toward a complete invariant description of all p-tuples (pairs included) over an arbitrary field, by separation rather than normal form. The paper does not claim to classify in the explicit sense, and does not say whether it contradicts the wildness of the problem.
events.object: No single object: the invariants are the ranks of linear matrix pencils built from the tuple, pencils of size at most n^3+n (Corollary 3.5). Two n×n tuples are simultaneously similar exactly when all these ranks agree (Theorem 1.1). Explicit as invariants; not a normal form.

events.what_happened: G. Ivanyos and Y. Qiao, 'On the orbit closure intersection problems for matrix tuples under conjugation and left-right actions', SODA 2023, pp. 4115-4126. Gives algorithms for the orbit-closure intersection problem for matrix tuples under simultaneous conjugation and left-right actions, outputting one-parameter subgroup cosets when the closures meet. NOT OPENED: the description comes from search summaries of the SZTAKI and UTS repository pages.
events.delivers: Algorithms deciding orbit-closure intersection for tuples under conjugation. A different problem from classifying orbits, so it does not classify pairs.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: orbit-closure intersection is not orbit classification.
events.direction: Neighbour: an orbit-closure decision problem for the same action. Settles nothing for the bullet.

events.what_happened: Y. Huang, 'Commuting matrices via commuting endomorphisms', arXiv 2404.19483 (v1 30 Apr 2024), math.RT. Proposes a counting framework for representation theory and reduces counts of commuting matrices to counts of endomorphisms of finite abelian p-groups; applications count finite modules over certain nonreduced curves over F_q and connect commuting triples to a conjecture of Onn. The abstract contrasts counting with classification and says some counts are tractable even when the classification is wild. Abstract opened.
events.revisions: v1 30 Apr 2024 as listed; later versions not checked.
events.delivers: Counting results for commuting matrices and modules over F_q. It classifies nothing and does not claim a classification of pairs under simultaneous similarity.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Discounted: a counting result for commuting matrices. Counts are not classifications, and the paper does not claim to classify pairs.

events.what_happened: V. Bondarenko, A. Petravchuk, M. Styopochkina, 'Polynomial similarity of pairs of matrices', arXiv 2408.04244 (v1 8 Aug 2024), math.RT. Defines polynomial equivalence (via polynomial maps with zero constant term and invertible Jacobian at the origin) on pairs of matrices and polynomial similarity on pairs of commuting nilpotent matrices. Main result: classifying these pairs up to polynomial similarity is wild, i.e. it contains the classical problem of classifying pairs up to similarity. The paper does not classify ordinary simultaneous similarity. A 2025 journal version was not found. Abstract opened.
events.revisions: v1 8 Aug 2024; later versions and journal status not found.
events.delivers: Wildness of a coarser analogue (polynomial similarity on commuting nilpotent pairs), by reduction to the classical pair problem. It classifies no pairs under the bullet's relation. The reduction goes from the analogue to the classical problem, so it does not give a solution of the classical one.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the bullet's relation (simultaneous conjugation) is not classified.
events.time_since_posted: about 26 months; no engagement found in searches
events.direction: Discounted: an analogue (different equivalence, commuting nilpotent subclass). Its result is a wildness claim for the analogue, consistent with the bullet's problem being hard. It settles no part of the bullet.

events.what_happened: Y. Qiao and X. Sun, 'Canonical forms for matrix tuples in polynomial time', arXiv 2409.12457 (v1 19 Sep 2024), FOCS 2024 (IEEE 65th Annual Symposium, Chicago, 27-30 Oct 2024), pp. 780-789, issue date 29 Nov 2024. For matrix tuples over a finite field F_q, gives a randomized Las Vegas algorithm computing canonical forms: Theorem 1.1 for rectangular tuples under left-right equivalence, time poly(n, m, ℓ, log q); Corollary 1.2 for square tuples under simultaneous conjugation, time poly(n, ℓ, log q), where ℓ is the tuple length. The paper defines canonical form as an algorithm output equivalent to the input and identical for all equivalent inputs. It describes classification of tuples under conjugation (two or more matrices) as wild, and states it does not claim a classification of pairs; the algorithm is not a list or parametrisation of orbits. Opened HTML in two calls; the second was truncated mid-proof of Lemma 5.4 in Section 5, so the final part of the paper, including any acknowledgements, was not read.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 19 Sep 2024 only as listed; FOCS 2024 proceedings version (issue 29 Nov 2024) is the peer-reviewed version.
events.delivers: A polynomial-time (expected, Las Vegas) algorithm computing a canonical form for simultaneous conjugacy of any tuple of n×n matrices, including pairs, over any finite field F_q. Over finite fields only: the algorithm decides conjugacy and classifies orbits algorithmically, but gives no explicit list or parametrisation, and makes no claim about infinite fields.
events.remains: Over infinite fields (including algebraically closed fields such as C), any classification of pairs in the explicit sense. Over finite fields, an explicit list or parametrisation of the orbits of pairs.

events.what_happened: K. Bongartz, 'On normal forms for the similarity classes of matrices and pairs of matrices', arXiv 2502.10926 (v1 15 Feb 2025; single version listed). Answers two questions from Arnold's Problems (1998). (1) Over any field, the similarity classes of n×n matrices have a representative system that is a finite disjoint union of affine subspaces. (2) For n > 1, the analogous statement fails for pairs of n×n matrices over any algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 (Theorem 3 in the HTML version: the action 'does not admit normal forms' of that type). A search summary described this paper as classifying pairs completely; that was contradicted by the opened text and is not relied on. A journal reference (Linear Algebra Appl. 743, 2026) appears only in a search summary; not verified.
events.delivers: A negative result: no representative system for simultaneous-similarity classes of pairs of n×n matrices (n ≥ 2) over algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0 can be a finite disjoint union of affine subspaces. It rules out one specific kind of normal form for pairs. It does not classify pairs and does not treat other kinds of normal form.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the paper gives no classification of pairs under simultaneous conjugation. It addresses only one type of normal form.

events.direction: Cuts against one natural route to a classification of pairs: no affine-subspace normal form. Consistent with the wildness benchmark. It does not contradict the bullet as stated, which asks for classification, not for that particular normal form.

events.what_happened: K. Bongartz and S. Friedland, 'Complete invariants for simultaneous similarity', arXiv 2601.00379 (math.RT; v1 1 Jan 2026, v2 14 May 2026, v3 21 May 2026). Comment: '12 pages, to appear in Advances in Mathematics' (an author statement; no journal acceptance was verified). Over an arbitrary field k, for the variety of p-tuples of n×n matrices with GL_n acting by simultaneous similarity: discrete invariants split the variety into finitely many locally closed GL_n-stable pieces; on each piece finitely many invariant morphisms to k separate orbits; the action then reduces to left multiplication by a product of GL_{l_i} on products of rectangular matrix spaces. The abstract states: 'Discrete and continuous invariants completely determine the orbits.' Theorem 4 (Section 4.3): A and B are equivalent iff E(r,A) = E(r,B) for all r in [n^2], where E are reduced row echelon forms of matrices F(r,A) built from minors of a linear map L(A,Y). The authors' own caveats (Section 1, Section 4.4, Section 6.3): the target Y is 'very big and growing fast with n and p'; 'we do not know the image of φ'; 'Their description seems to be a hard problem'; 'It is clear that our stratification is not the solution to this problem because neither the strata nor the quotients are explicitly described'; Section 6.3 gives four remarks that the problem is 'at least very hard if not impossible' (no normal forms already for pairs of complex 2×2 matrices; quotients conjectured rational only for n ≤ 4; a smooth variety with free PGL(3)-action and no geometric quotient; undecidability of a first-order theory of pairs). An AI referee on Pith (grok-4.3) reviewed it on 22 May 2026 (see checked_by). Full HTML read via fetch; no truncation note.
events.revisions: v1 1 Jan 2026; v2 14 May 2026; v3 21 May 2026. The changes between versions were not read; Pith's AI review (22 May 2026) may refer to v2 or v3.
events.delivers: Per the abstract and Theorem 4: complete separating (discrete plus continuous) invariants for all p-tuples of n×n matrices over an arbitrary field under simultaneous similarity, including pairs. By the authors' own account this is not an explicit classification: the strata and quotients are not explicitly described, and the stratification 'is not the solution to this problem'.
events.remains: An explicit description of the orbit space, meaning explicit strata, quotients, or normal forms. The authors say these are not given; by their own account the problem is 'at least very hard if not impossible'.

Also one minor concern on notation. The page also contains a 'simulated authors' rebuttal' that Pith labels simulated, not an author response

events.doubts: (1) Pith's AI referee's major concern: the completeness claim depends on the uniform discrete-invariant construction for arbitrary fields, including finite and positive-characteristic fields; the referee says it fails without algebraic closure if only sketched (automated review, not a human). (2) The authors' own Section 6.3 says the stratification is not a solution and that the problem is 'at least very hard if not impossible'. (3) No journal acceptance is verified beyond the authors' 'to appear' comment. (4) No citing work was found. The v2 and v3 changes were not read.
events.direction: Toward the bullet being solved in a separating sense: a claim of complete invariants for all tuples over any field, pairs included. The authors' own text says this is not an explicit classification and that the problem is very hard. Whether a complete separating invariant of this kind counts as classifying the bullet is for the judging pass. Closest in content to Derksen et al. 2021 (pencil ranks) but with a different construction; whether the two are compared in the text was not checked.
events.object: No single object. A stratification of the variety of p-tuples into finitely many GL_n-stable locally closed pieces, with finitely many invariant morphisms on each piece separating orbits. Theorem 4 uses reduced row echelon forms of matrices built from minors of a linear map. The strata are not explicitly described (Section 6.3).

disputes.summary: Whether Friedland (1983) already gave complete invariants for simultaneous similarity of pairs. Secondary descriptions disagree (complete versus finite ambiguity). The 2026 Bongartz-Friedland preprint claims complete invariants for all p-tuples over arbitrary fields; the 2021 Derksen-Klep-Makam-Volčič result (pencil ranks, published Adv. Math. 2023) also claims a separating invariant family over arbitrary fields. Neither the text of Friedland 1983 nor a citation of Derksen et al. in the 2026 preprint was checked.

summary: Searches (63 queries; Wikipedia list entry and article, arXiv, journal pages, Pith referee pages, OpenAI manuscript repository, lab announcements and expert digests) found no AI-attributed event bearing on this bullet, and a set of mathematical events in and before the window. The bullet sits under Algebra in Wikipedia's list with a link to the Wild problem article, which defines wildness by containment of the pair problem (Belitskii-Sergeichuk 2003); the wildness benchmark is pre-window and is not itself an event in the window. In the window: (i) Qiao and Sun (arXiv Sept 2024; FOCS 2024) give a randomized polynomial-time canonical form for conjugation of square matrix tuples over finite fields. The authors call the classification wild and do not claim to classify pairs, so this is algorithmic rather than an explicit classification, and it is restricted to finite fields. (ii) Bongartz (Feb 2025) proves the pair problem for n ≥ 2 over algebraically closed characteristic-0 fields has no normal form of the affine-subspace type, a negative result about one kind of normal form. (iii) Bouarga and Charkani (Feb 2025) fully describe the centralizer of one matrix over any field and say this solves 'a weaker version of the Wild Problem'; the body was unreadable and the weaker version is not stated, so this is unresolved. (iv) Bongartz and Friedland (arXiv Jan 2026, 'to appear in Advances in Mathematics') claim complete discrete-plus-continuous invariants for p-tuples over any field. Their own §6.3 says the stratification 'is not the solution', that the problem is 'at least very hard if not impossible', and that the strata and quotients are not explicitly described. The only review is an automated Pith referee (grok-4.3, 22 May 2026) with a major concern about the arbitrary-field completeness step; Pith states no human has reviewed it. Pre-window, the closest candidates for resolution are Derksen-Klep-Makam-Volčič (arXiv Sept 2021, Adv. Math. 2023), who show pencil-rank invariants separate simultaneous similarity orbits of n×n tuples with no field restriction in their Theorem 1.1, and Friedland (1983), whose content is disputed between secondary sources (finite ambiguity versus complete); the Friedland text was not reachable. Both are recorded as events. The record also contains several subclass results (Hua 2023, Bondarenko-Futorny-Petravchuk-Sergeichuk 2020, Bondarenko-Zubaruk 2023, commuting-tuple counts) and discounted analogues (polynomial similarity, unitary variants, centralizers, commuting-family criteria, geometric varieties). Close calls: (a) Qiao-Sun versus 'classification' — the result is algorithmic over finite fields, the authors call the problem wild, and the answer depends on whether an algorithmic canonical form counts; (b) Bongartz-Friedland versus 'classification' — the invariants are complete by the authors' account but not explicit by their own account; (c) Derksen et al. (2021) — a complete separating family with no field restriction, but indexed by pencils of size up to n^3+n rather than an explicit list. Corrections to search-summary claims, which the primary text did not bear out: a search summary said Bongartz (2025) 'solves completely and explicitly' the pair classification, but the arXiv text says the reverse; a search summary said the 2026 Pierce-Birkhoff AI paper contains a 'matrix-pair construction in dimension 72', but its arXiv abstract is math.AG with no matrix pairs. The Bouarga 'weaker version' relaxation attributed to Wang 2019 by a search summary was not found in the abstract. AI: none of the events names an AI system in the sources read; the OpenAI October 2026 release (719 manuscripts, openai/math) was screened in full via its CONTENTS.md catalogue (automated, six chunks) and contains no title on matrix pairs, conjugation, quivers or wild classification.
competing_reading: The strongest case that the bullet has been resolved in the window: Bongartz and Friedland (arXiv Jan 2026, to appear in Adv. Math.) state that discrete and continuous invariants 'completely determine the orbits' of p-tuples of n×n matrices over any field, which is what the bullet asks for in the separating sense; combined with Derksen et al. (2021) this is already a complete invariant description, and the classification question is answered by separation rather than explicit normal form. The strongest case against: 'classification' in the wild context means an explicit parametrisation or list of normal forms; the authors of the complete-invariants paper say their strata and quotients are not explicit and that their construction is not a solution; Bongartz (2025) shows no affine-subspace normal form exists for pairs; Qiao and Sun's algorithm works only over finite fields and gives no explicit list; and the problem is wild by the Belitskii-Sergeichuk benchmark, which the completeness claims do not contradict but do not circumvent in an explicit sense.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Whether Bongartz-Friedland's uniform discrete-invariant construction works over arbitrary fields, including finite and characteristic-p fields, as the Pith AI referee questions; whether a human referee or Advances in Mathematics accepts it; and what v2 and v3 changed. (2) Whether the judging standard counts separating invariant families (Derksen et al. 2021; Bongartz-Friedland 2026) as classification of pairs, given the authors' own statements that the orbit space is not explicit. (3) The full text of Bouarga and Charkani (2025) to identify the 'weaker version of the Wild Problem'. (4) The text of Friedland (1983) and the MRC report, to settle whether the 1983 invariants are complete. (5) The rest of Qiao and Sun (FOCS 2024) to confirm the acknowledgements and the finite-field scope, and whether any later work extends the algorithm to infinite fields.

judgement.why: The statement asks for a classification of pairs under simultaneous conjugation, which in the wild-problem sense means an explicit description of the orbits (normal forms or a parametrisation). The separating-invariant results (Derksen et al. 2021; Bongartz-Friedland 2026) answer a changed question, deciding equivalence rather than describing the orbits. Bongartz and Friedland say outright that their stratification 'is not the solution to this problem', so both are variant. Qiao-Sun's canonical-form algorithm over finite fields was the closest call: one could read it as a finite-field case, but the authors disclaim classifying pairs and an algorithmic canonical form is a different notion from classification, so variant. Bongartz 2025 rules out one kind of normal form, which bounds nothing and classifies nothing, so none. Counting, polynomial similarity, centralizers and variety geometry are variants. Subclass classifications that predate the snapshot (Hua, BFPS, Bondarenko-Zubaruk) are cases. The 1983 and 2003 refereed papers and the 2020 journal paper are digested via journal acceptance, as is FOCS acceptance. No AI was involved in any event.
judgement.doubts: Qiao-Sun could reasonably be read as a case (classification over finite fields, given algorithmically); I read it as variant because the authors disclaim classification. Bongartz-Friedland is still not human-reviewed, and Pith's automated concern about arbitrary fields is not a knock-down. Friedland 1983 was never read.
